title: Growing cabbage microgreens
subtitle: Mild brassica cotyledons with a blue-green tint, cut in 8 to 12 days
excerpt: Cabbage microgreens produce mild, slightly waxy blue-green cotyledons that combine well with more assertive microgreens in a mixed tray. The cycle is 8 to 12 days on a 25 cm indoor tray.
sourceNotes: UMass Extension microgreens guides (open-access). Cornell Cooperative Extension indoor growing material. Standard microgreen-growing practice synthesised from extension service material.

glossaryTerms.definition: Watering by setting the growing tray inside a second tray filled with water, allowing the growing medium to draw moisture up from below. Keeps the seedling surface dry and reduces mould and damping-off risk in microgreen trays.

A fungal condition where seedling stems collapse and rot at the soil surface. Caused by Pythium, Fusarium, and Rhizoctonia species in warm, wet, poorly-ventilated conditions. Common in overcrowded or overwatered microgreen trays.

content.text: Cabbage microgreens are an indoor, year-round tray crop that reaches the cutting stage in 8 to 12 days. The cycle follows the standard brassica microgreen pattern: sow, blackout for three days, light for 5 to 9 more days, cut when cotyledons are fully expanded. The flavour is mild and slightly waxy, less peppery than radish or mustard.
Cabbage microgreens are useful as a base in a mixed microgreen tray. Their mild flavour does not compete with radish or rocket; the blue-green cotyledons add colour contrast.

Light: a bright south-facing windowsill works in spring and summer. In winter a grow light at 15 to 20 cm above the tray, running 14 hours a day, improves colour and stem straightness. Cabbage microgreens in low winter light are paler and slower to green up after the blackout phase.
Temperature: 18 to 22°C. Cabbage germinates readily at room temperature and tolerates a cooler kitchen (15 to 16°C) with a slightly extended cycle.
Day 0: sow. Pre-dampen seed compost or coir and fill the tray to within 1 cm of the rim. Scatter cabbage microgreen seed at 15 to 20 g per 25 cm tray. Press gently into contact with the medium.
Days 1 to 3: blackout. Cover with a weighted second tray. Cabbage takes a full three days in the blackout phase before shoots reach 2 to 3 cm.
Day 4 onward: light. Cotyledons green up within 24 hours.
only: set the tray inside an outer tray with 1 to 2 cm of water and let the medium soak it up from below.
Days 8 to 12: cut. When cotyledons are fully open, upright, and 5 to 8 cm tall, cut 1 cm above the medium with scissors. Use fresh or refrigerate for up to two days.

attrs.heading: Troubleshooting
attrs.intro: Common problems on cabbage microgreen trays.

items.symptom: Stems rot at the base; tray has a sour smell
items.fix: Bottom-water only. Discard and start fresh. Ensure the room has some airflow.

items.symptom: Cotyledons remain pale and fail to green up
items.cause: Insufficient light after the blackout phase.
items.fix: Move to a brighter position or add a grow light. Cabbage takes longer to green up than radish; allow 24 to 36 hours in good light before concluding there is a problem.

items.symptom: Sparse germination in the first three days
items.cause: Old or coated seed, or medium too dry during germination.
items.fix: Test seed viability in a damp cloth germination test before a full tray. Ensure the medium is uniformly damp before sowing.

content.text: Use untreated cabbage seed. Standard vegetable cabbage seed is often fungicide-coated. Microgreen suppliers stock untreated varieties in suitable pack sizes.
risk is low. Bottom-water only and don't let the medium stay wet.
